options.text: Eigen vectors can never be the zero vector.
If $\vec{x}$ is an eigen vector of a matrix $A$, then $2 \vec{x}$ is also an eigen vector of $A$.

questions.solution:

Also, if an eigen value of a matrix is zero, then the determinant of the matrix is zero which means the matrix is singular

C is correct.For proof of option C , refer https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1557665/is-the-scalar-multiple-of-an-eigenvector-also-an-eigenvector-for-a-particular-ei

Always, the rank of a matrix A$_m$$_x$$_n$ $<=$ $min(m,n)$ . So option D is correct.

questions.qtext:
Which of the following vectors are eigenvectors of the matrix: $\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 3 & 6\\
2 & 1 & 4\\
1 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right]$
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 19)
Just check if $A \vec{x}=\lambda \vec{x}$ for some scalar $\lambda$. It turns out only $\left[\begin{array}{c}-2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{array}\right]$ is an eigenvector, with eigenvalue $1 .$
Source solution 2 (score: 14)
Method-1) you can check each vector in $Ax = \lambda x$ and see that only option B comes satisfies this equation with $\lambda = 1$.

A) $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 6 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ -3 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix}$ ❌

B) $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 6 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ ✅

C) $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 6 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -27 \\ -19 \\ -15 \end{bmatrix}$ ❌

Method-2) Put all the 3 vectors given in the options and find the matrix multiplication, it will be faster.

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 6 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & -5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -2 & -27 \\ -3 & -2 & -19 \\ -5 & 1 & -15 \end{bmatrix}$

we can see that columns of resultant matrix contains vectors in the form $Ax$ and only column 2 in the resultant matrix is of the form $\lambda x$. so option B is correct.

$$
\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{s}\left[\begin{array}{l}

$$
We do some unknown elementary row transformations on $A$ and get the following matrix $R$ -
$$
R=\left[\begin{array}{llll}
1 & 0 & \mathrm{a} & \mathrm{b} \\
0 & 1 & \mathrm{c} & \mathrm{d} \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{array}\right]
$$
What will be the values of $a, b, c,$ and $d?$
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D

Selected solution (score: 27)

Given $x$ is the solution for $Ax=0$ hence it is also a solution for $Rx=0$.

Putting $s=1$ and $t=0$, the $x$ we get is $\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$.

$\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$ should satisy $Rx=0$.

$\left[\begin{array}{llll}1 & 0 & \mathrm{a} & \mathrm{b} \\ 0 & 1 & \mathrm{c} & \mathrm{d} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right] = 0$

  • $1+a = 0 \implies a = -1$
  • $ 1+c = 0 \implies c = -1$

Similarly

Putting $s=0$ and $t=1$, the $x$ we get is $\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]$.

$\left[\begin{array}{llll}1 & 0 & \mathrm{a} & \mathrm{b} \\ 0 & 1 & \mathrm{c} & \mathrm{d} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = 0$

  • $b = 2$
  • $d = 1$

Hence Answer is – A, B, C, D.

questions.qtext:
Consider the vectors $\mathbf{u}=\left[\begin{array}{l}1\\
1\end{array}\right], \mathbf{v}=\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\
c^{2}\end{array}\right], \mathbf{b}=\left[\begin{array}{l}1\\
c\end{array}\right]$, where $c$ is a constant.
Consider two statements.

  • $\mathrm{S} 1: \;c=1$ is the ONLY possibility where $b$ is a linear combination of $u$ and $v$.
  • $\mathrm{S} 2:\; c=-1$ is the ONLY possibility where $b$ is NOT a linear combination of $u$ and $v$.

Which of the following is/are true?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 77)
To find out if $\mathbf{b}$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ we have to check if there are numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}$, such that $x_{1} \mathbf{u}+x_{2} \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$.
We can check if this system of linear equations has a solution by looking at the echelon form of the augmented matrix $[\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \mid \mathbf{b}]$.
After Row operations on this matrix we obtain -
$$
[\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \mid \mathbf{b}]=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & c^{2} & c
\end{array}\right]\overset{-R 1+R 2}{\longrightarrow}\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 \\
0 & c^{2}-1 & c-1
\end{array}\right] .
$$
We know that solution will not exist if we have $[0,0 \mid$ NonZero $]$ as any row. Otherwise, solutions will always exist.

We want $c^{2}-1$ to be zero and $c-1$ to be nonzero. This is possible only when $c=-1$.

This means, that only at $c=-1$ the solution doesn't exist otherwise always exists.
Source solution 2 (score: 27)
Say $b$ is linear combination of $u$ and $v$ .So we can write ,

$c_{1}u+c_{2}v=b$

$c1\begin{pmatrix} 1\\ 1\\ \end{pmatrix}$+$c_{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1\\ c^{2}\\ \end{pmatrix}$=$\begin{pmatrix} 1\\ c\\ \end{pmatrix}$

$\begin{pmatrix} c_{1}+c_{2}\\ c_{1}+c_{2}c^{2}\\ \end{pmatrix}$=$\begin{pmatrix} 1\\ c\\ \end{pmatrix}$

So we can write ,

$c_{1}+c_{2}=1$

So ,$c_{1}=1-c_{2}$ --------------------------(1)

$c_{1}+c_{2}c^{2}=c$-----------------(2)

Putting (1) in (2) we get ,

$1-c_{2}+c_{2}c^{2}=c$

or,$1-c_{2}(1-c^{2})=c$

or,$c_{2}=\frac{1}{1+c}$

$c_{1}=\frac{c}{1+c}$

So for any $c$ except $c=-1$ we can get coefficients such that $b$ is linearly combination of $u$ and $v$.

So correct answer is (B) .

options.text: Suppose an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ has $n$ pivot columns. Then for each $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$, the equation $A \mathbf{x}=\mathrm{b}$ has at most one solution.
Suppose $A x=b$ has a solution, the solution is unique if and only if $A x=0$ has unique solution.
If $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix and $A x=0$ has a unique solution, then $A x=b$ is consistent for every $b$ in $\mathbf{R}^{m}$.
If for some matrix $A$, and some vectors $x$ and $b$, we have $A x=b$, then $b$ is linear combination of columns of $A$.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, D

Source solution 1 (score: 20)
A) TRUE, case 1: $m=n$, in this case the matrix is full rank with $n$ pivots so unique solution (exactly $1$).

case 2: $m > n$, in this case there will be atleast one row where, $[0 \quad 0 \dots 0 \mid b_k]$ exist so depending on value of $b_k$ which is a component of vector $b$, the existence of solution will vary. If $b_k$ is also $0$ ultimately leading to $[0 \quad 0 \dots 0 \mid 0]$ then solution exists and if $b_k$ is non-zero leading to $[0 \quad 0 \dots 0 \mid \text{non-zero}]$ then solution doesn't exist.

hence, atmost $1$ solution in this case.

B) TRUE, If $Ax = b$ has a solution then that means $b$ is a linear combination of columns of matrix $A$. now knowing that $Ax = 0$ has unique solution that tells us that only trivial solution can reduce columns of matrix $A$ to $0$. so, they are linearly independent and hence, unique solution for $Ax=b$.

C) FALSE, For example, if $A=\left(\begin{array}{lr}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array}\right)$, then $A x=0$ has only the trivial solution, but $A x=\left(\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right)$ has no solution.

D) TRUE, $Ax$ will produce a vector that is the linear comination of columns of $A$ according to the matrix-vector multication so if $Ax = b$ then $b$ is the resultant linear comination of columns of $A$.

questions.solution:

Source solution 1 (score: 30)
This question will clear many things.

Dimension of the matrix could easily be calculated by the degree of characteristics polynomial = $6$.

One short answer for those who are from a maths background and understand vector spaces well.

The null space of $A$, which coincide with the eigenspace corresponding to $0 ,$ could have dimension $1$ or $2.$ Thus $\operatorname{rank}(A)$ could be $4$ or $5.$



Detailed answer:

$\lambda = 0,0$. It means, corresponding to $\lambda = 0$ we can have at most $2$ linearly independent eigenvectors. (This is because geometric multiplicity is less or equal to arithmetic multiplicity)

We do have $Ax=\lambda x$ and if $\lambda$ is zero then $Ax=0$ where $x$ is eigen vector corresponding to $\lambda = 0$.
as we stated before, there are ATMOST two possible linearly independent $x’s$ are possible. And obviously, there will be at least one eigenvector.
So LI eigevectors corresponding to $\lambda = 0$ are $1$ or $2$.



$Ax=0$ has just $2$ solutions, it means free variables ATMOST are $2$. Hence nullity = free variables = ATMOST $2$ = $1$ or $2$.

Rank = $6$ – nullity = $4$ or $5$.

questions.qtext: Let $A$ be $n\times n$ matrix with real coefficients. Which of the following is/are true?

options.text: A must have an even number of non-real eigenvalues.
If $v_{1}, v_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ are eigenvectors of $A$ with different eigenvalues $\lambda_{1} \neq \lambda_{2}$, then $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ are linearly independent.
If $v_{1}, v_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ are eigenvectors of $A$ with different eigenvalues $\lambda_{1} \neq \lambda_{2}$, then $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ are orthogonal.
The eigenvalues of $A B$ are the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ and $B$.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 22)
A. A must have an even number of non-real eigenvalues.
Solution: True, either with or without multiplicity. It's easier to explain why the answer is yes without multiplicity: if $\lambda=a+b i$ is an eigenvalue with $b \neq 0$ and complex eigenvector $v \in \mathbb{C}^{n}$, then its complex conjugate $\bar{\lambda}=a-b i$ must also be an eigenvalue, with eigenvector $\bar{v}$ (this means we take the complex conjugate of every entry of $v$ ). So the non-real eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs.

B. If $v_{1}, v_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ are eigenvectors of $A$ with different eigenvalues $\lambda_{1} \neq \lambda_{2}$, then $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ are linearly independent.
Solution: True. If $c_{1} v_{1}+c_{2} v_{2}=0$, then applying $A$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
A\left(c_{1} v_{1}+c_{2} v_{2}\right) &=c_{1} A v_{1}+c_{2} A v_{2} \\
&=c_{1} \lambda_{1} v_{1}+c_{2} \lambda_{2} v_{2} \\
&=0 .
\end{aligned}
$$
Subtracting $\lambda_{1}\left(c_{1} v_{1}+c_{2} v_{2}\right)=0$ gives $c_{2}\left(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}\right) v_{2}=0$, and since $v_{2} \neq 0$ (being an eigenvector) and $\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2} \neq 0$ (by assumption), we get $c_{2}=0$. This gives $c_{1} v_{1}=0$, and since $v_{1} \neq 0$ this gives $c_{1}=0$.

C. If $v_{1}, v_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ are eigenvectors of $A$ with different eigenvalues $\lambda_{1} \neq \lambda_{2}$, then $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ are orthogonal.
Solution: False. For example, $A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array}\right]$ has two eigenvalues $1,0$ with eigenvectors $\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$ and $\left[\begin{array}{c}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right]$ which are not orthogonal, although they are linearly independent. More generally, specifying a pair of linearly independent vectors $v_{1}, v_{2}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and a pair of distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_{1} \neq \lambda_{2}$ for them uniquely specifies a matrix $A=P D P^{-1}$, where $D$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}$ and $P$ is the matrix whose columns are $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$. In this construction there's no reason for $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ to be orthogonal.
However, this is true if $A$ is symmetric $\left(A=A^{T}\right)$.

D. The eigenvalues of $A B$ are the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ and $B$.
Solution: False. This statement should seem quite suspicious because the eigenvalues of a matrix don't come in any distinguished order, so there's no distinguished way to match up an eigenvalue of $A$ with an eigenvalue of $B$ to multiply them and get an eigenvalue of $A B$. For an explicit counterexample, take
$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
0 & 1 \\
0 & 0
\end{array}\right], B=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
0 & 0 \\
1 & 0
\end{array}\right], A B=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 0
\end{array}\right] .
$$
The eigenvalues of $A$ and $B$ are both just $0,$ but $A B$ has eigenvalues both $0$ and $1 .$

$B$ is not invertible for any values of $a, b, c$.
$B$ is invertible for all values of $a, b, c$.
$A$ is not invertible for any values of $a, b, c$.

questions.solution:
Answer: B, A

Source solution 1 (score: 12)

Use the formula for the determinant of a $3 \times 3$ matrix.
$$
\operatorname{det}(A)=1-a b c+a b c+c^{2}+b^{2}+a^{2}=1+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} \geq 1
$$
and
$$
\operatorname{det}(B)=0-a b c+a b c+0+0+0=0 .
$$
Thus

  • $A$ is invertible for all values of $a, b, c$.
  • $B$ is not invertible for any values of $a, b, c$.
Source solution 2 (score: 7)

$B=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &a &b \\ -a& 0 &c \\ -b& -c & 0 \end{bmatrix}$

$B^{T}=-\begin{bmatrix} 0 &-a &-b \\ a& 0 &-c \\ b& c & 0 \end{bmatrix}=-B$

So B is skew symmetric matrix .

Now, we know $\left | B \right |=\left | B^{T} \right |$

So, $\left | B \right |=\left |- B\right |$

or, $\left | B \right |=(-1)^{3}\left |B\right|$

or,$\left | B \right |=-\left | B \right |$

or,2$\left | B \right |=0$

or,$\left | B \right |=0$

So ,$B$ is not invertible . (By looking we can answer as determinant of odd order skew symmetric matrix is $0$.)

$B=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &a &b \\ -a& 1 &c \\ -b& -c & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Try converting it in echelon form ,

$B=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &a &b \\ 0& 1+a^2 &ab+c \\ 0& ab-c & 1+b^{2} \end{bmatrix}$ [ $R_{2}← R_{2}+aR_{1}$ ,$R_{3}← R_{3}+bR_{1}$]

$B=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &a &b \\ 0& 1+a^2 &ab+c \\ 0& 0 & (1+b^{2})-\frac{a^{2}b^{2}-c^{2}}{1+a^{2}} \end{bmatrix}$

$B=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &a &b \\ 0& 1+a^2 &ab+c \\ 0& 0 & 1+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} \end{bmatrix}$

Now as $1+a^2$ and $ 1+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} $ can never be zero so rank of this matrix is $3$ . so this matrix is invertible .

So correct answer is (A) and (B).

questions.qtext: Let $A$ be $5 \times 4$ matrix. If all solutions of $A x=0$ are scalar multiple of one nonzero vector then what will be the rank of $A?$
questions.solution:
Answer: 3

Selected solution (score: 21)

Given : All solutions of $Ax = 0$ are scalar multiple of one non-zero vector.

$\implies$ Number of linearly independent solutions of $Ax=0$ is $1$.

$\implies$ nullity(A) is $1$.

$\therefore$ rank(A) = $4-1 = 3$.

Answer :- 3.
